item.title: NZDUSD Technicals: The NZDUSD is stretching to a new high since September 23.
item.description:
The NZDUSD is stretching to the upside, reaching its highest level since September 23. Buyers have been rebuilding the technical picture after the pair’s decline from the August 21 high at 0.59868 to last Wednesday’s low at 0.55645.

That recovery has developed one step at a time. First, the price broke above a downward-sloping trendline. Then it moved above its 100- and 200-hour moving averages and started to put some distance between the price and those technical barometers. A subsequent break above the swing area between 0.56256 and 0.56333 gave buyers another reason to push higher.

Today, the pair cleared another swing area between 0.5673 and 0.5686. The encouraging part for buyers was what happened next: the price rotated back toward the top of that area, found support, and turned higher again. That successful retest helped propel the pair to a session high near 0.5704.

The buyers are making a play. But there is another important hurdle ahead.

What comes next?

The next key upside target is the 38.2% retracement of the decline from the August 21 high at 0.57258.

Why does that level matter? After a strong trend move lower, I look at the 38.2% retracement as a minimum benchmark for judging whether buyers are making a more meaningful challenge to that trend.

The recovery has improved the shorter-term bias, but a move above 0.57258—and the ability to stay above it—would strengthen the case that buyers are taking back more control. If the price stalls below that retracement, the broader move can still be viewed as a correction within the preceding downtrend.

The distinction matters. A rally gives buyers an opportunity. Getting above key resistance and staying above it provides stronger technical confirmation.

Where is the risk for buyers?

On the downside, the low of the broken swing area near 0.56736 is now an important support level. Buyers would want to see that level hold to keep the breakout intact.

A more conservative risk level comes against the rising 100-hour moving average at 0.56637. That moving average is moving closer to the swing-area support. A break below both would weaken the bullish technical picture and put more pressure on buyers.

For now, the progression favors the buyers: break resistance, hold it on a retest, and extend toward the next target. Their job is to keep that sequence going.

In the video above, I walk through those technical steps and explain how I use them to define bias, risk, and targets—so you can understand the mindset behind the trade and the levels that would change the view.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bitcoin shows some buying life as risk-on flows return and push the digital currency higher
item.description:
Bitcoin buyers are making a play to the upside after sellers could not extend the price lower.

The price is currently trading near $84,518, up around $1,700, or 2.11%. The rally gained momentum after breaking above the 100- and 200-hour moving averages near $82,100. Buyers have now pushed above last week’s swing high near $84,178, giving them another technical break in their favor.

The buyers have taken back control in the short term. Now they need to hold it.

Where is the risk for buyers?

The closest risk-defining level is the broken swing high at $84,178. When the price breaks above resistance, traders want to see that level become support. Staying above it would keep the buyers firmly in control. Moving back below would take some of the momentum out of the breakout.

For traders giving the move more room, $83,000 provides another reference point. Below that, the 100- and 200-hour moving averages near $82,100 become the more important support area. A move back below both would weaken the bullish technical picture.

Those levels offer different amounts of breathing room, but more room also means more dollars at risk. Traders need to match their position size to the risk they choose.

What comes next on the topside?

The next upside target is $85,578, the lower boundary of an upper swing area within the broader range that has confined trading since September 18. Above that, the focus shifts to the range high at $87,374.

Getting above $84,178 is progress. Getting above $85,578 would be another step. Ultimately, buyers need to break and stay above $87,374 to open the door beyond the broader trading range.

The lesson is that a failed move in one direction can create an opportunity in the other. Sellers had their shot to extend lower. They missed. Buyers have responded by taking the price above the hourly moving averages and last week’s swing high.

In the video above, I take a look at the bitcoin breakout, the levels buyers need to hold, and the next targets that will help determine whether this rally has more room to run.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: US treasury sells $13 billion of 20 year bonds at a high yield of 5.469%
item.description:
• Prior auction yield 5.420%

Details of the 20 year auction Jesus Christ

  • WI level at the time of the auction: 5.460%

  • High yield: 5.469%

  • WI level at the time of the auction: 5.460%

  • Tail: 0.9 basis points vs the average of 0.2 basis points

  • Bid to cover: 2.73X vs the average of 2.62X

  • Directs: 31.6% vs the average of 22.9%

  • Indirects: 58.2% vs the average of 65.2%

  • Dealers: 10.3% vs the average of 11.9%

Auction grade: C

A mixed auction overall. The Treasury had to pay 0.9 basis points above the WI yield to get the bonds sold, a larger concession than the average of 0.2 basis points. Indirect demand was also softer than average. On the positive side, bid to cover was stronger, direct bidders stepped up, and dealers were left with less supply than usual. Those demand measures help offset the weaker pricing, but the larger tail keeps this from earning an above-average grade.

Generally speaking, the 20 year issue is not a strong part of the yield curve. With the 20 year yield higher than the 30 year yield at 5.4133%, and also higher than the 10 year yield of 5.106%,suggests less overall demand by investors. In a normal positive slope yield curve which we have, the yield should be lower than the 30 year but higher than the 10 year.

item.title: European stocks close higher, but French yields hit their highest since 2002
item.description:
As London and European traders head home, the major European stock indices are closing higher. Germany’s DAX led the advance, while the UK’s FTSE 100 lagged but still finished with a modest gain.

The closing snapshot shows:

  • German DAX: +342.67 points or 1.35% at 25,647.10

  • France CAC: +83.19 points or 1.06% at 7,921.69

  • UK FTSE 100: +19.88 points or 0.19% at 10,752.87

  • Spain IBEX: +231.10 points or 1.21% at 19,323.50

  • Italy FTSE MIB: +572.32 points or 1.17% at 49,643.68

One headline getting attention came from a US official who said Russia accepted the American proposal for a trilateral meeting with Ukraine. Subsequent reporting says the Kremlin agreed to renewed technical-level talks on or after November 10, potentially in Abu Dhabi. That is a step forward, although agreeing to meet leaves the difficult negotiations ahead.

For traders, the importance stretches beyond the diplomatic headlines. Russia matters for oil, refined products, and natural gas. My view is that credible progress toward peace could give Trump more political room to work with Putin on energy and economic issues. But that room depends on results. A meeting alone will not remove the political backlash or resolve the uncertainty around supplies and sanctions.

The markets need peace to make that story more durable. Progress could ease some of the geopolitical premium in energy prices and improve confidence around future supply. Another disappointment would leave traders vulnerable to the next headline and the next shove. Oil and European natural gas remain markets to watch closely as the diplomatic process develops.

Zelenskyy has also been working the diplomatic channels. In Oslo on Tuesday, he met Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, and US envoy Steve Witkoff, with Jared Kushner joining remotely. The discussions covered security guarantees, sanctions, reconstruction, air defense, and a possible meeting between the leaders. Zelenskyy also confirmed that US early-warning intelligence for Russian missile attacks was working again. Ukraine’s position included support for a mutual halt to attacks on energy infrastructure.

That puts the focus on what follows the meetings. The diplomatic activity gives traders something to work with, but concrete commitments—and whether the parties follow through—will determine whether the optimism lasts.

France, meanwhile, remains a problem in the bond market. Its benchmark 10-year yield pushed above 5%, reaching its highest level since 2002, as investors continued to question the country’s fiscal position. Higher borrowing costs add to the challenge of bringing its finances under control.

In the supplied afternoon snapshot, France’s 10-year yield was 5.009%, up 6.4 basis points. Germany’s equivalent yield was only 0.4 basis point higher at 3.421%, leaving the French premium at roughly 159 basis points. That divergence is the warning. French stocks participated in today’s rally, but the bond market continues to demand more compensation for holding French debt.

Elsewhere, Spain’s 10-year yield was 2.5 basis points higher at 4.079%, and Italy’s rose 4.2 basis points to 4.589%. UK gilts moved the other way, with the 10-year yield down 4.9 basis points at 5.381%.

US stocks were also higher as Europe headed for the exits, with technology leading. In the latest broad-market snapshot:

  • Dow: +136.58 points or 0.26% at 52,632.46

  • S&P 500: +40.62 points or 0.53% at 7,753.19

  • Nasdaq 100: +375.15 points or 1.27% at 29,865.43

The slightly earlier snapshot showed the Nasdaq Composite up 296.49 points, or 1.12%, at 26,721.31.

US Treasury yields were mixed, with the front end modestly higher and longer maturities lower. The 2-year yield was 4.793%, up 0.6 basis point, the 5-year 4.934%, essentially unchanged, the 10-year 5.109%, down 0.8 basis point, and the 30-year 5.416%, down 1.0 basis point.

In currencies, the dollar was mixed. The euro slipped 0.15% to 1.1219, while the Australian dollar led gains against the greenback, with AUDUSD up 0.33% at 0.7025. GBPUSD was marginally higher at 1.3385, USDJPY edged lower to 158.11, and USDCHF rose to 0.8252.

Commodities: Oil reverses lower and breaks below $97

Crude oil has seen another sizeable reversal as traders weigh the latest diplomatic headlines and their implications for energy supplies. After reaching $100.40, the price tumbled to a fresh session low of $96.63. That is a $3.77 move from the high and, technically, takes the price below the $97 swing level.

The currenr price was last near $96.83, down $1.34 or 1.36%. The sellers have taken more control, but they now need to keep the price below $97. Stay below, and the break keeps the downside in focus. Move back above and hold above, and the sellers will have had their shot below support without sustaining the momentum.

The Russia-US-Ukraine diplomatic developments add another layer to the energy story alongside the ongoing US-Iran negotiations. Credible progress toward peace could ease concerns about supply disruptions. However, traders have already seen how quickly optimism can reverse when the next headline raises doubts. The headlines provide the shove. The technical levels help traders define the risk.

Elsewhere, spot gold was modestly higher near $4,132.50, up $7.04 or 0.17%, while silver fell approximately 0.79% to $57.52. Natural gas was 0.48% lower near $6.572, and bitcoin gained approximately 1.80% to $84,441.

Overall, equity buyers have the better hand today. France’s rising borrowing costs and the unfinished peace negotiations remain two stories that can quickly test their conviction.

item.title: AUDUSD Technicals: The AUDUSD runs into the 100 day MA and finds willing sellers.
item.description:
The AUDUSD has staged a steady recovery since reaching 0.6894 last Thursday, its lowest level since early July. There have been modest corrections along the way, but buyers have continued to push higher. Today, the AUD is the strongest of the major currencies against the greenback.

However, that rally has reached an important technical hurdle.

The price extended to its 100-day moving average at 0.70332, with the session high reaching 0.7036 before sellers leaned against that level.

The buck stopped there.

The price has since rotated lower to 0.70185, taking it below the 38.2% retracement of the decline from the September high at 0.7025, and below the lower boundary of a swing area at 0.7020. That gives sellers an opening, but they still need to build on it.

For traders looking for a high to be in place, the downside roadmap is straightforward:

  1. Stay below the 100-day moving average at 0.70332. That keeps the rejection intact and gives sellers a level against which to define their risk.

  2. Build momentum below 0.7025–0.7020. The break has occurred. Now sellers need to keep the price below that area and extend lower.

  3. Break below last week’s high at 0.70125. Moving back below that former breakout level would weaken the buyers’ case further.

If sellers can work through those steps, the next downside target comes at the 0.6989–0.6994 swing area, followed by the 100- and 200-hour moving averages below.

Conversely, a move back above the 100-day moving average at 0.70332, followed by an ability to stay above it, would put buyers back in position to challenge the 200-day moving average at 0.7047. Above that, the next target is the 50% midpoint of the decline from the September high at 0.70654.

The educational takeaway is that reaching resistance and confirming a reversal are two different steps. The 100-day moving average has attracted sellers, but the rejection alone does not establish a lasting high. Sellers need follow-through below the nearby retracement and swing levels. Without that progress, this could still be a correction within the rebound from last week’s low.

In the video above, I take a look at the AUDUSD’s rejection at the 100-day moving average, the levels sellers need to break to gain more control, and what would put buyers back in charge.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: USDCAD Technicals: The USDCAD pair pushes higher off of 100 day MA support. What next?
item.description:
The USDCAD formed a double top near 1.42984 last Wednesday before sellers took control. Over the next five trading days, the pair fell to a low of 1.4032—a decline of about 266 pips.

That move took the price below its 100-day moving average near 1.4041 yesterday. However, sellers could not sustain the break, and the price rebounded. They had their shot below a key technical level. They missed.

In the Asian and European sessions today, sellers tried again. The price dipped below the 100-day moving average, now near 1.4042, but only reached 1.4039 before bouncing back above it. A second attempt below the moving average also failed to find follow-through selling.

Today’s rebound developed more momentum than yesterday’s, taking out the early Asian session high and extending toward the broken 38.2% retracement and swing level at 1.40818. The high reached 1.4081, where sellers leaned against resistance. The pair has since rotated back toward 1.4066.

Buyers and sellers have now defined their levels.

On the downside, the 100-day moving average at 1.4042 remains the key barometer. Buyers have defended that area on two consecutive days. Staying above it keeps the recovery attempt alive. A sustained break below would shift the bias back toward the sellers, with the lows at 1.4039 and 1.4032 ahead of the 50% midpoint at 1.40149. Get below that midpoint, and the door opens for further selling.

On the topside, the 1.40818 retracement and swing level is the hurdle. Sellers have shown they are willing to defend it. Buyers need to get above—and stay above—that level to strengthen the recovery and open the door toward the falling 100-hour moving average near 1.4112.

The lesson for traders is that a break needs follow-through. Moving below the 100-day moving average gave sellers an opportunity, but the quick recoveries showed they could not maintain control. Buyers have earned some breathing room, but they still have work to do at 1.40818.

For now, support is holding below and resistance is holding above. Traders are waiting for the next shove.

In the video above, I take a look at the USDCAD’s decline, the failed breaks below the 100-day moving average, and the levels that will help determine whether buyers can extend the recovery or sellers regain control.

item.title: Crude oil inventories show a draw of -3.060M versus estimate of -0.82 million drawdown
item.description:
US weekly crude oil inventories fall 3.060 million barrels vs 0.820 million draw expected

  • Crude oil: −3.060 million barrels vs −0.820 million expected. Prior −8.557 million.

  • Gasoline: −2.952 million barrels vs −0.443 million expected. Prior +3.518 million.

  • Distillates: +1.675 million barrels vs −1.162 million expected. Prior −2.527 million.

US crude oil inventories fell more than expected in the Energy Information Administration’s weekly report. Gasoline stocks also recorded a larger-than-expected draw, but an unexpected build in distillates provided an offset.

Last night’s private inventory data

The American Petroleum Institute (API) figures, as reported by Julianne Geiger in the supplied screenshot, showed:

  • Crude oil: −4.93 million barrels vs −1.3 million expected.

  • Gasoline: −2.0 million barrels.

  • Distillates: −2.6 million barrels.

  • Cushing inventories: +900,000 barrels.

The official crude draw was smaller than the private survey indicated, while the gasoline draw was larger. The biggest difference was in distillates: the EIA reported a 1.675 million-barrel build, compared with the API’s 2.6 million-barrel draw.

Quick analysis: The crude and gasoline draws lean supportive for oil prices, but the distillate build takes some shine off the report. Compared with last night’s private figures, today’s official numbers give oil buyers a less clear-cut bullish story. Inventory changes also reflect refinery activity and trade flows, so draws alone do not establish stronger demand. One weekly report is unlikely to change the Fed’s outlook, although sustained energy-price gains could add to inflation concerns.

What this report measures: The EIA’s weekly petroleum report tracks US oil inventories, refinery activity and supply flows. A draw means stocks declined; a build means they increased. Traders compare the official figures with expectations and the earlier API private survey for clues about supply and demand.

item.title: US stocks open higher as earnings and AI demand take center stage
item.description:
US stocks are opening higher, giving buyers the early advantage as investors digest earnings from SpaceX and Netflix, a stronger outlook from Super Micro Computer, and fresh AI announcements from Nvidia.

  • Dow Industrial Average: The Dow is modestly higher to kickstart the day

  • S&P 500: The broader S&P is up 18 points or 0.24%

  • Nasdaq Composite: The tech heavy Nasdaq composite index is leading with a gain of 140 points or 0.56%

SpaceX climbs as AI and Starlink drive growth

SpaceX shares are trading higher by around 8.6% following a strong third-quarter report. Revenue surged 161% from a year ago to $14.6 billion, while net income reached $4.4 billion, reversing a year-earlier loss of $1.1 billion. Its Super Intelligence segment generated $7.6 billion in revenue, while Starlink finished the quarter with 13.6 million consumer subscribers, an increase of 1.6 million from the previous quarter. The growth is substantial, but so is the investment: quarterly capital spending totaled approximately $19.6 billion.

The price of SpaceX shares are back above the 200 and 100 hour MAs at $153.81 and 157.51 respectively. The low today held the 100 hour MA with a low at $158.20. Staying above is bullish and keeps the buyers in control. 

Netflix falls as guidance overshadows an earnings beat

Netflix is seeing the opposite reaction, with shares down 4.5%. Third-quarter earnings of $0.87 per share beat expectations of $0.82, while revenue increased 11.8% to $12.87 billion. However, fourth-quarter guidance disappointed, with projected earnings of $0.67 per share below expectations of $0.73 and revenue of approximately $13.44 billion also below forecasts. Netflix additionally reduced its full-year advertising revenue outlook to approximately $2.7 billion from $3 billion, citing a slower rollout of some advertising capabilities.

The reaction provides a useful reminder for traders: an earnings beat does not guarantee a higher stock price. Investors also weigh what comes next against what was already expected. For Netflix, concerns about the outlook are carrying more weight than the latest quarter’s earnings beat.

Netflix shares are trading at the lowest level since August 2024 with a low today aof $64.10.  The high price reached in July 2025 reached $134.12.  

SMCI raises its outlook on stronger AI demand

Super Micro Computer is adding to the positive AI backdrop after sharply raising its preliminary revenue estimate for the September quarter. The company now expects fiscal first-quarter revenue of $18.5 billion to $19.5 billion, up from previous guidance of $14.5 billion to $15.5 billion, primarily reflecting stronger demand for AI platforms. At the midpoint, that is a $4 billion increase, or nearly 27%.

The improvement also extends to profitability. SMCI now expects gross margins of 12% to 12.5%, compared with its previous range of 10.4% to 10.8%, primarily because of its customer and product mix. Higher revenue alongside better margins gives investors two positives to consider ahead of the full quarterly results on November 3.

SMCI’s update provides evidence that demand for AI systems is running ahead of its earlier expectations. That brings Nvidia into focus as well. The servers need computing power, and Nvidia’s latest announcements highlight how the company is expanding its reach across the infrastructure supporting that demand. Shares are trading up near 14% in early trading.

Nvidia expands its AI partnerships

CEO Jensen Huang announced a series of partnerships during his keynote address and said Nvidia has invested nearly $10 billion across Europe over the past year, including investments in 14 European startups in the past week.

Among the announcements, Google Cloud plans to scale Nvidia’s Vera Rubin infrastructure to 960,000 GPUs. Partnerships with Schneider Electric and Infineon focus on the data centers and power systems needed to support that expansion, while work with Nokia aims to bring more AI capabilities into telecommunications networks.

The announcements extend beyond the chips themselves. Nvidia is also expanding its work with Dell, HPE and CrowdStrike across enterprise AI and security. For the broader stock market, that highlights how AI spending reaches across suppliers, infrastructure providers and business applications. Investors will continue to judge how effectively those investments translate into revenue and earnings.

For Nvidia traders, that provides the fundamental backdrop. Now the price action needs to confirm the story. Today’s gains give buyers their opportunity, but getting above resistance—and staying above it—is what would strengthen the technical case.

Looking at the hourly chart, Nvidia has tested its 100-day moving average, currently at $214.62, several times since last Wednesday. The price dipped below that key longer-term barometer on Wednesday, Friday and again yesterday. Each time, however, sellers failed to build downside momentum.

The sellers had their shot. They could not get the price to break and run.

Today, buyers are pushing back. Nvidia has traded as high as $222.16 and is currently near $221, up about $4.50 on the day. That moves the price away from the 100-day moving average and gives buyers some breathing room. However, holding support is only the first step. There is still work to do before buyers can claim more control.

The next hurdle comes near $225, where the 200-hour moving average and a broken upward-sloping trendline converge. Getting back above that area would be a positive step. Above that, the 100-hour moving average at $227.55 becomes the next target.

Those levels provide a roadmap. Move above $225 and then $227.55—and stay above them—and the technical picture improves. Buyers would have reclaimed both hourly moving averages and moved back above the broken trendline, opening the door for a potential run toward the all-time high at $243.37.

Until then, this remains a rebound from important support with resistance still overhead. If sellers stall the recovery at those hurdles, they keep the opportunity to push back toward the 100-day moving average.

The lesson for traders is straightforward: a successful defense of support gives buyers a chance. Reclaiming resistance helps confirm they are taking control. Nvidia has accomplished the first part. Now buyers need to follow through.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Crude oil futures reacted to the news headlines keeps traders focused on the technicals
item.description:
Crude oil futures have been on a roller coaster, with competing headlines sending traders scrambling in both directions.

Yesterday, the price surged toward $101.40 before tumbling to around $95.30, then rebounding again. Reports of progress toward inspections of Iranian nuclear facilities encouraged selling, but conflicting reports and denials helped reverse that move.

The headlines keep changing. The uncertainty remains.

Negotiations continue, but an agreement remains elusive

The overnight headlines offered another reminder of why traders need to remain flexible. Iranian Foreign Minister Araghchi said indirect negotiations are continuing through intermediary countries, including Pakistan and Qatar. He also outlined a proposal that includes reopening the Strait of Hormuz if the US fulfills its commitments. Those are Iran’s stated terms, however, rather than confirmation of an agreed reopening.

Meanwhile, Iran’s president said dialogue cannot take place alongside a blockade and threats. A separate report carried by Al Hadath said Iran rejected American demands conveyed through Pakistan. President Trump offered a more optimistic assessment, saying the US is doing “very well” with Iran, while indicating that a final decision remains on how he wants to win the war.

The Saudi-Houthi fighting adds another supply-risk concern. Progress between Washington and Tehran would be significant, but traders also need to watch whether that separate conflict eases.

For the market, the problem is straightforward: a headline can change expectations quickly, and the next headline can reverse them just as fast.

The $97–$98.48 swing area is the immediate battleground

Today’s price action has been a smaller version of yesterday’s volatility, with a high near $100.40 and a low at $96.92.

That low briefly broke below the $97 lower boundary of an important swing area before buyers pushed the price back above it. With crude trading near $97.20 at the time of writing, the price is back inside the $97.00–$98.48 swing area, but remains near its lower end.

The sellers had their shot below $97. They could not sustain the break. That gives buyers something to lean against, but there is still work to do before they can claim more control.

The first hurdle is the 100-hour moving average at $97.65, which sits inside the swing area. Buyers need to get above—and stay above—that moving average to improve the short-term picture.

Above that, $98.48 becomes the next test. Clearing that upper boundary would open the door for a move back toward the recent highs stretching from $99.27 to $101.40, including today’s high at $100.40.

The steps matter: reclaim the moving average, clear the swing area, and then look for follow-through toward the highs.

Below $97, the 200-hour moving average comes into focus

Conversely, a sustained move below $97.00 would weaken the rebound and put the rising 200-hour moving average at $95.31 back in focus.

The price has held above that moving average since October 12, with yesterday’s decline providing a test that attracted buyers. That makes it an important reference for the broader hourly trend.

A break below it—and an inability to recover—would give sellers more control and leave the market vulnerable to a deeper correction.

Further down, the 38.2% retracement of the July 2–September 15 advance comes in at $91.60. The 50% midpoint at $86.93, near where the October 6 bottom formed, provides another longer-term reference.

Those are deeper downside levels. The immediate decisions remain around $97.00 and the two hourly moving averages.

The trading lesson: follow the levels and demand follow-through

This remains a trading market. A move toward one technical level can stall, reverse, and send the price back toward the previous level. Traders need to respect that two-way risk.

That is why simply breaking a level is only part of the story. Can the price stay beyond it? Does the next target get reached? Does a pullback hold the level that was just broken?

Those are the clues that help distinguish a headline-driven spike from a move that is building momentum.

For now, the technical roadmap provides structure while the fundamental story keeps shifting. What we want to see is a clearer fundamental direction supported by the price action. Until then, take it one level at a time and be ready for the next shove.

In the video, I walk through the crude oil technical ladder and the levels buyers and sellers need to break to take more control.

item.title: Morning Kickstart: Dollar mixed as oil swings on conflicting US-Iran headlines

The markets are starting Wednesday with a familiar problem: the US and Iran are reportedly still talking, but the headlines continue to pull traders in different directions.

Crude oil has already traded above $100 and back below it. US Treasury yields are modestly lower, stock futures are pointing higher, and the dollar is mixed. There is movement, but there is no consistent message across markets.

In the morning video above, I take a look at the three major currency pairs—EURUSD, USDJPY and GBPUSD—from a technical perspective. For each pair, I outline the bias, the risk-defining levels and the targets that would give either the buyers or sellers more control.

At 7:30 AM ET, crude oil was trading at $98.66, up $0.80 on the day. The high reached $100.40, while the low extended to $97.91. That is a $2.49 trading range, with the price well off its high but still higher on the day.

Giuseppe Dellamotta’s latest oil analysis outlines the competing forces: a breakthrough could reduce the supply-risk premium, while a continued stalemate would keep that risk in the market.

The latest headlines underline the uncertainty:

  • Iranian Foreign Minister Araghchi says indirect negotiations are continuing through intermediary countries, including Pakistan and Qatar.

  • Araghchi says Iran’s proposal includes reopening the Strait of Hormuz if the US fulfills its commitments. Those are Iran’s stated terms, rather than confirmation of an agreed reopening.

  • Iran’s president says dialogue cannot take place alongside a blockade and threats.

  • A separate report carried by Al Hadath says Iran rejected American demands conveyed through Pakistan.

  • President Trump says the US is doing “very well” with Iran, while indicating that a final decision remains on how he wants to win the war.

Meanwhile, the Saudi-Houthi fighting remains another supply-risk concern. Progress between Washington and Tehran would be significant, but traders also need to watch whether that separate conflict eases.

For traders, the distinction matters. A proposal is a step. An agreement is another step. Implementation is another. The price action needs to confirm which step the market believes has actually been taken.

US stock futures point higher

item.title: Connecting the dots: How rising government bond yields could hurt your retirement savings
item.description:
Just imagine you have a decent sum of money and that you are looking for good investment to get into. Now, someone comes up to you and offers you a relatively safe investment that pays 5% a year. That doesn't sound too shabby, no? Especially when you don't have to pick your brain in trying to find the next big stock market winner.

Well, that's essentially what government bonds are offering in this market. With Treasury yields hovering around 5% lately, that proposition is looking rather attractive.

So, what happens when investors can earn decent returns without taking much risk? All of a sudden, everything else has to work a little harder to compete with what those bonds are offering.

I mean, think about it. If you can earn 5% from a US government bond, would you really want to take on the additional risk of investing in stocks for a similar return? Probably not. To compensate you for wanting to take on that risk, you'd want something extra in return. And that is where the trouble begins for stock markets.

When government bond yields rise, investors generally demand higher potential returns from riskier investments too. That can also mean paying less for company shares today, even if the businesses themselves haven't changed much.

Besides that, there's another problem to consider. Let's not forget that companies borrow money too. And when government borrowing costs rise, corporate borrowing rates often follow.

Let's take an example where a company wants to borrow $1 million to build a new factory. At 4% interest, that's $40,000 annually. At 7%, it's $70,000. That's an extra $30,000 every year that could otherwise have gone towards hiring workers, expanding the business, or even rewarding shareholders.

Now, imagine that very same thing happening across hundreds or even thousands of companies. Slower investment leads to weaker profits and that in turn puts pressure on stock valuations. That is not quite something that sounds good for your retirement portfolio, does it?

And here's the part I think people sometimes overlook. You don't have to own government bonds directly to feel the impact of all that. Your pension fund, retirement account, or long-term investment portfolio would almost certainly have a mix of both stocks and bonds.

So, rising yields can push down the market value of existing fixed-rate bonds while also weighing on share prices at the same time. Thus, that can leave retirement savings facing pressure from both sides of the equation.

Now, higher yields aren't exactly all bad. There is the fact that new bond investments can offer better income, which may benefit long-term savers. But for someone who might be approaching retirement, the timing of a market downturn can be especially painful.

As much as we might not think about it, the very fact of life investing is that a government borrowing more expensively today could very well end up affecting how comfortably you retire tomorrow.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: European markets steady for now but widening bond yield spreads offer a warning
item.description:
European equities are keeping steadier so far today with France's benchmark CAC 40 index even holding up by 0.3% on the session. Meanwhile, the euro is also only slightly lower against the dollar but is still holding above the 1.1200 level at around 1.1215 currently. That suggests traders are not quite rushing for the exits just yet.

That being said, I wouldn't be too quick to mistake the calmer mood for an improvement in the underlying risks for European markets. Not especially when the bond market is hinting at a different mood.

The France-Germany 10-year yield spread has widened further to around 158 bps today, marking its highest level since 2011. And if you look at the chart, we're now revisiting levels last seen during the height of the Eurozone sovereign debt crisis.

That's hardly a reassuring comparison, even if we are not quite talking about a repeat of those very same circumstances just yet.

In any case, the widening spread reflects the growing premium investors are demanding to hold French debt over German bonds. And with France's fiscal troubles and political uncertainty showing little signs of easing, there isn't much reason for bond investors to feel more comfortable at this stage.

So, what's next from here?

It will be important to watch out for any concerns about how this story could develop into something that is not just France anymore. And we might already be getting some early hints of that.

The Italy-Germany 10-year yield spread has also widened to nearly 119 bps today, threatening to retest the highs around 120-125 bps seen at the start of this month. If that spread continues to push higher alongside the France-Germany spread, it would suggest that investors are becoming more cautious about euro area sovereign debt more broadly. In other words, the story is starting to become more than just a French one.

That is where the risk of wider market contagion starts to creep into the picture. In turn, that could potentially weigh more heavily on European equities and the euro while complicating the ECB's policy outlook.

For now, the calm in broader markets is a welcome relief. However, I would be paying much closer attention to what is happening beneath the surface. With yield spreads at the risk of blowing up, there's every risk that this recovery in market sentiment could be a short-lived one.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Macro pulse: Is the BOJ about to raise interest rates at the worst possible time?
item.description:
I don't think anyone would want to the be in the BOJ's shoes right now. On the one hand, inflation pressures are giving policymakers every reason to keep raising interest rates. But on the other hand, Japan's economy is already dealing with expensive energy imports and a weak yen - not to mention a very uncertain global outlook.

If that isn't problematic enough, then here's the kicker. The inflation pressures that are building aren't exactly the kind that the BOJ has been hoping for.

The central bank has spent decades in trying to nurture a healthier cycle of rising wages, stronger consumer spending, and sustainable price increases. For the most part, those efforts went nowhere. And it took a global economic reset from the Covid pandemic to finally give Japan a get-out-of-jail-free card.

Remember, Japan spent much of the last thirty years struggling with stagnant wages and prices. Businesses were reluctant to raise prices, workers weren't getting any meaningful wage increases, and consumers had grown accustomed to things staying relatively cheap.

Then came the Covid pandemic, followed by global supply chain disruptions and a surge in commodity prices. Suddenly, businesses had little choice but to raise prices as inflation started making its way back into the Japanese economy. Initially, that was largely cost-push inflation too. But it also helped break Japan's long-standing reluctance to raise prices, while workers began pushing harder for higher wages to keep up with living costs.

And for a while, it looked like Japan was finally getting the sort of inflation that policymakers had spent years trying to achieve. But amid the US-Iran conflict this year, much of the latest surge in price pressures is coming from the other direction.

Higher oil prices and import costs are forcing businesses to pay more, with those increases eventually being passed on to consumers. Once again, it's another story of cost-push inflation. And unlike wage-driven inflation, it doesn't necessarily leave households with more money to spend. In fact, it is quite the opposite actually.

And Japan's latest trade figures underline the problem. The country recorded a ¥2.8 trillion trade deficit for the April to September period, more than double the roughly ¥1.2 trillion deficit recorded a year earlier. That is largely driven by a 20.4% surge in imports as soaring energy import costs take their toll.

This is where things get particularly awkward for the BOJ. The central bank has spent years trying to get inflation going but now it has to worry about whether the latest bout of price pressures might actually undermine the wage-driven recovery it has worked so hard to achieve.

So, where does that leave interest rates?

For now, markets are virtually ruling out a rate hike in October but are pricing in roughly a 74% probability of another move in December. That fits with the sort of messaging we have seen from the BOJ as of late, with the tightening pace still sticking around once every quarter in order to manage the risks of inflation overshooting.

Having said that, raising interest rates isn't going to make oil prices any cheaper. And while a stronger yen could provide some relief, that's hardly a given when Treasury yields remain elevated and the dollar continues to attract demand from traders across the globe.

All the while, higher borrowing costs could end up squeezing domestic spending and business investment at a time when Japan can ill afford another drag on growth.

Damned if you do, damned if you don't.

It's kind of ironic. The BOJ spent decades trying to escape an economy where prices wouldn't rise. But now, it risks tightening policy because prices appear to be rising for all the wrong reasons.

I'm not saying that another rate hike would necessarily be a mistake. However, I would argue that the margin for error is getting smaller. And for a central bank that has spent so long trying to get inflation right, the last thing it needs is to get the timing wrong.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Why Treasury yields move together but become more volatile further out the curve
item.description:
Treasury yields are primarily driven by expectations for the future path of Federal Reserve monetary policy. This relationship is especially strong at the front end of the yield curve, where yields are closely linked to expectations about how the Fed will adjust interest rates over the near-term. However, monetary policy expectations remain important even at the long end of the curve. The difference is that longer-term yields are also more sensitive to changes in the economic outlook, inflation expectations and the compensation investors demand for holding long-duration bonds, called term premium.

The front-end is driven by monetary policy expectations

The 2-year Treasury yield is one of the most useful indicators of market expectations for Federal Reserve policy. If markets begin to expect the Fed to raise interest rates in the coming months, the two-year yield will generally rise. Conversely, if economic data weakens or inflation moderates, markets will start to price in rate cuts and the 2-year yield will generally fall.

The key point is that markets are forward-looking. Treasury yields reflect expectations for future short-term interest rates over the life of the bond. Consequently, yields will move well before the Fed actually changes its policy rate. That doesn't mean the market will always be right. Sometimes the market gets things wrong, but the change in expectations still drives yields higher or lower depending on the economic context and incoming information.

The long-end is still driven by monetary policy expectations

The 10-year and 30-year Treasury yields are often framed as though they move independently of the Fed. But that's misleading. Expectations for monetary policy remain a fundamental driver of longer-term yields, but their influence is more complex because investors must consider a much longer economic horizon.

A longer-term Treasury yield can be decomposed into two components: expected future short-term interest rates and a term premium. The first component links long-term yields directly to monetary policy expectations. If investors expect the Fed to maintain restrictive policy for longer, or believe that short-term rates will settle at a higher level over the coming decade, longer-term yields will generally face upward pressure.

The second component helps explain why long-term yields can move significantly even when expectations for the federal funds rate change very little. The term premium can rise when uncertainty about inflation increases for example, as investors will demand greater compensation for bearing duration risk. Changes in the supply and demand for Treasuries can also influence this premium, although it's a very minor part. The term premium is not seomthing that is observable or can be accurately calculated. It changes based on the economic context. 

Chart: Federal Funds Rate (black), 2y yield (red), 5y yield (green), 10y yield (violet), 30y yield (blue)

Long-term yields are more sensitive to growth and inflation

Although monetary policy expectations matter across the entire yield curve, the further we move out in maturity, the more economic developments can influence the outlook for interest rates over the longer run.

Suppose we get a very strong US PMI report that changes expectations about growth. The data might lead markets to expect more Fed rate hikes, pushing the 2-year yield higher, but the implications for the 10-year yield can extend beyond the next few Fed meetings. Stronger growth could imply a higher equilibrium real interest rate, stronger underlying demand and potentially greater inflationary pressure. If investors think that the economy can sustain higher interest rates over the long run, long-term yields may rise by more than the 2-year yield.

This is what generally leads to a bear steepening of the curve as long-term bonds fall faster than short-term bonds. That's exactly what happened after the September's US Flash PMI, as you can see in the chart below.

The same logic applies to inflation. A temporary increase in inflation might change expectations for the next few Fed meetings, but a persistent inflation shock can alter expectations for inflation over many years. Investors may also demand a higher term premium because of increased uncertainty.

The reverse is also true. A deterioration in the growth outlook can push yields lower as markets anticipate monetary easing. This is why before an economic slowdown or even a recession, the 10-year yield falls faster than the 2-year yield. This can happen even during a Federal Reserve tightening cycle if the markets think that the central bank overtightened and will have to cut interest rates sooner than expected.

This is why longer-term yields can experience larger swings than shorter-term yields. They reflect not only the expected response of monetary policy in the near-term but also changing views about the economy over a longer horizon.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Chart of the day: Gold price eyes $4,100 support as $4,200 resistance keeps bulls in check
item.description:
Gold continues to find itself on the defensive in the past few weeks, as the precious metal is unable to gather much reprieve from both a fundamental and technical perspective.

On the former, the bond market continues to play a key role. With 10-year Treasury yields hovering above 5%, the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset like gold is rather difficult to ignore. And that angle currently outweighs the fact that gold has historically been a solid hedge against geopolitical and inflation risks.

Meanwhile, the technicals are also reflecting that struggle quite clearly. Looking at the 4-hour chart, sellers have repeatedly defended the $4,200-20 region since the start of October. The 100-period moving average (red line) has also consistently capped recovery attempts, with the latest rejection leaving gold hovering around $4,114 today.

The daily chart also tells a similar story with gold price action continue to hold below the key daily moving averages, keeping sellers in control:

The $4,200-20 region is the immediate hurdle to any upside push, while the $4,100-17 area is now the key support zone to watch.

In other words, we are seeing a consolidation phase for gold price and one that has clear technical levels defining it. That leaves us with two possible scenarios.

For the bulls, defending the $4,100-17 region is the first priority. But in looking to the upside, they need to muster a convincing break above $4,200-20 first. Only then can the bulls start taking aim at the 100-day moving average at around $4,232 currently before looking to $4,300 next. As for catalysts, easing Treasury yields would certainly help alongside continued central bank demand for the precious metal in the bigger picture.

For the bears, a firm break below $4,100 would expose the $4,000 psychological mark and potentially the July low near $3,960 as the next targets. As for catalysts, the very fact that 10-year Treasury yields continue to keep above 5% is a strong reason to keep broader markets on edge and put gold in a tight spot.

But for now though, the predicament is relatively straightforward. Gold price remains caught between $4,100-17 and $4,200-20 with there being neither enough conviction from safety hedge to offset the pressure from higher borrowing costs; vice versa.

So until something gives way, it's a bit of a waiting game. Buyers have the $4,100-17 region to defend, while sellers are keeping a firm grip on the $4,200-20 area. But with Treasury yields still elevated, I would argue that the burden remains on gold bulls to prove they can turn things around.
